debris.notes: Acres of shredded multi-layer insulation still bunched on its standoffs — the lightest thing in the envelope by a wide margin, and it tears if you look at it wrong.
Several bus panels folded into one another by the cascade; the commonest thing in the low envelope and the piece a break-even run is built out of.
Half a wing of shattered cells still on its hinge — light for its bulk, and the glass goes if the shield does.
Structural spine off a comms bus, kinked but sound; four slots uncrushed makes it the first real hold-space decision.
An expended apogee motor, burnt through and empty — dense scrap steel in one tidy slot, and the first grab that moves the mass dial.
A folded ten-metre reflector rib cage — the magnet skids off it; crane cable only, so the shipping slice sees it and cannot have it.
Gold-plated wire mesh balled up around its former spar; worth real money by mass and it will not survive a hard flare.
A vented nickel-hydrogen pack on its mounting rails — two of these are most of a starter hold's mass budget.
A momentum wheel welded solid by its own bearing failure; a whole lot of dense metal in a single slot.
A titanium helium bottle split along its weld — the densest single-slot grab available to a starter hold.
A heat-pipe panel peeling apart at the bondline; four slots, glass-brittle, and the last fragile piece before the shipping slice gets serious.
The carbon backbone of a full array wing, cells stripped away — the bread-and-butter mid-envelope haul.
An imager tube with its primary mirror starred through; one slot, high value per kilo, and its uncrushable flag is a field rather than a sentence.
A berthing ring sheared off its tunnel — forged alloy, awkward shape, and no argument about whether it is worth the trip.
Four RCS nozzles on a common manifold, valves fused shut; the best mass-per-slot in the middle third.
A crew-module end dome caved in on itself — crane cable only, and a standing advertisement for the hold you cannot afford yet.
A composite-overwrapped bottle blown open at the boss; heavy, sturdy, and it eats four slots uncrushed.
Navigation optics in a machined housing, baffle crushed — dense, delicate, and the piece that teaches you to deploy the chute early.
A whole attitude-control tray, three wheels still bolted down — one grab that costs a starter hold two slots of mass budget.
A charred fairing tip off an upper stage, its ablator crazed through — ironic cargo, and it burns first when the shield goes.
A flight computer bay cracked open, boards still seated; the richest fragile piece below the top third and a genuine gamble on your flying.
Tungsten-laced shadow shielding off a nuclear tug — the top third's baseline haul, and it doubles your reentry problem on its own.
A precision high-gain reflector, its face split across the rim — enormous value and no tolerance for a late chute.
Molybdenum accelerator grids arced together into a solid brick; one slot, brutal mass, and half durability the whole way down.
Thirty metres of deployable truss, sheared at the root — crane cable only, and the heaviest ordinary object in the envelope.
A platinum-catalysed cell stack off a crewed vehicle, casing scorched through — the top third's honest workhorse.
A vacuum-jacketed helium dewar with its inner vessel collapsed; heavy, fragile, and worth the whole trip if it lands intact.
A regeneratively cooled nozzle peppered by the cascade — the heaviest thing a hand magnet can legally take home.
A crew hatch with its pane starred, hanging just under the module — the last thing you pass on the way to Armstrong's prize, and a real temptation to overload.

Apollo-era service module hanging at the ceiling, older than the cascade and still whole — one slot, roughly double the ship's mass, and the only object in the catalog that degrades pristine to damaged to scrap instead of breaking. fixed_objective true: it is placed, never rolled, and no weighted sampler may draw it.

revision_notes: Balancer concern 1, floor mass_kg: taken, and the floor population is now heavier. Every hand-tetherable piece in the bottom third was re-massed upward and the middle third was raised with it so the curve stays smooth: the spawn-weighted hand-tetherable mass of the bottom third goes from 17.4 kg to 37.9 kg per slot, a factor of 2.2, so a 6-slot starter hold weighs 227 kg rather than 104 kg and the dry mass the audited doubling rule forces moves from 105 kg to 227 kg — staged ballistic coefficient 21 to 46 against the Researcher's floor of 100. I did not reach the balancer's suggested 5x, and the reason is arithmetic rather than preference: 87 kg per slot at the floor would make the bottom third 89% of the top third's 97.8 kg per slot, collapsing the catalog's top-to-bottom mass factor from 5.4 to 1.15 and deleting the one property my charter calls central. 2.2x is the largest raise that leaves a legible gradient, and it is a real move toward the rule rather than a restatement of my last position.

What still does not close, stated so the next agent does not have to rediscover it: at 37.9 kg per slot the doubling rule read against a starter hold of floor scrap still implies a 227 kg rocket, beta 46. Read against a full hold at the top of the band — 7 slots of the top third's 97.8 kg per slot, 685 kg — the same rule implies a ~685 kg ship at beta 140, which agrees with the Researcher's assumed 600 kg staged dry mass and with the GDD's own flown full-hold figure of ~1,398 kg. The remaining gap is which hold the rule reads, not how heavy the floor pieces are; the floor cannot carry it without becoming the top third.

Balancer concern 2, armstrongs_module mass_kg: the same change is my answer, because it is the only legal direction. The module's ~3,600 kg is fixed by my charter in three places and the endgame rule is measured against it, so it cannot come down. The hold-filling population came up at the floor, where there was room. It cannot come up at the top: the top third's masses are pinned by GDD 2.2's flown heat table, where a full hold at ~1,398 kg peaks at 203.7 against the module's 268.8. Raising the top third to the ~300 kg per slot the two doubling sentences jointly require would put a 7-slot top-of-band hold at 2,100 kg — above the module's own mass — and the 32% plunge window the whole endgame rests on would be gone. The parachute ladder's 72-1,150 m2 span is the honest cost of a win condition that is 21.8x the heaviest ordinary piece and 29.5x the heaviest hand-tetherable one; that ratio is the design, not a catalog defect.

Balancer concern 3, oversized pricing: agreed and unchanged, recorded for both of us. No oversized piece can enter a hold in the shipping slice, so economy.size_class_base_value's oversized entry is unreadable content-side; leaving it priced is the right call if the crane magnet is ever restored.

What moved and what did not. Changed: mass_kg on all 21 pieces below 203,333 m, and five bottom-third spawn weights (crumpled_panel_stack 18 to 16, bent_truss_section 15 to 14, cracked_battery_pallet 11 to 12, seized_reaction_wheel_housing 12 to 13, burst_pressurant_sphere 10 to 12) which shift weight toward the dense floor grabs and hold the bottom third's fragile fraction at exactly 0.100. Unchanged: every id, every altitude_m, every size_class, every fragile and uncrushable flag, fixed_objective, all nine top-third masses and all top-third weights. Note prose changed only on the four pieces whose old sentence contradicted the new mass. band_summary is recomputed from the array as it now stands.

Bottom third arithmetic, so the auditor can check it without re-deriving: masses 15, 24, 21, 30, 36, 82, 34, 46, 50, 54, 48 sum to 440 over 11 pieces, mean 40.0. Weights 3, 16, 2, 14, 12, 2, 2, 12, 13, 12, 2 sum to 90; the fragile ids (torn_foil_blanket, cracked_solar_array, shredded_antenna_mesh, delaminated_radiator_fin) carry 3+2+2+2 = 9, so 9/90 = 0.100. Middle third: masses sum 805 over 10, mean 80.5; fragile weight 12 of 69 = 0.1739. Top third is unchanged at 4,449 over 9 = 494.33 and 10 of 40 = 0.250.
design_notes: The catalog's top-to-bottom mass factor is now 2.65 rather than 5.4 — the top third's ordinary mean is 106.1 kg against the bottom third's 40.0 kg — and that compression is the price of the balancer's finding, paid deliberately. A better haul is still visibly a harder ride home: per slot, the top third's hand-tetherable population runs 97.8 kg against the floor's 37.9 kg, so filling a hold at the ceiling still costs two and a half times the landing mass of filling it at the floor.

Mass climbs monotonically with altitude with no cliff: no adjacent ordinary pair differs by more than 1.45x, with one deliberate exception at the very floor. torn_foil_blanket at 15 kg sits 1.6x below the panel stack above it because the catalog needs one genuine featherweight — a shredded insulation blanket that reads as free mass — and its spawn weight of 3 keeps it an oddity the player meets rather than a hold-filling staple. Every other piece in the bottom third is dense scrap by design, which is what makes 37.9 kg per slot true of a hold actually filled at the floor.

The oversized entries are massed at roughly twice their local altitude neighbourhood (82, 148, 165 kg) rather than by their bulk. Size class is a volume-and-slot statement, not a mass statement, so they sit above the trend without distorting the mass-versus-altitude curve they live inside, and the catalog stays coherent if the crane magnet is ever restored to scope.

Armstrong's module is authored explicitly rather than approximated by the heaviest ordinary piece. The heaviest ordinary object is the severed boom mast at 165 kg and the heaviest hand-tetherable one is the engine bell at 122 kg, so the module stands 21.8x and 29.5x above them. The endgame rule that the module cannot plunge is therefore measured against the win condition and not against a nose cone, and its ~20% margin is real.

The reported top-third mean_mass_kg of 494.33 is the plain average the charter asks for and it includes Armstrong's module at 3,600 kg, which is why it reads an order of magnitude above the middle third. The ordinary-piece figure is 106.1 kg. Anything downstream reasoning about hold mass should use the ordinary population; the module is a single fixed objective above the shipping slice, and it carries fixed_objective true so a sampler can filter it.

Fragile fractions are spawn-weighted, not counted, and they were recomputed after this revision: bottom 9/90 = 0.100, middle 12/69 = 0.1739, top 10/40 = 0.250. The counts alone would read 4/11, 4/10 and 4/9 — an almost flat gradient — which is exactly the failure mode the charter names. The weights carry the gradient.

Every size class and the fragile flag appear inside the shipping slice, the bottom two thirds. Small, medium and fragile all show up in the first 40 km of the band; the oversized class is met at 86,500 m as a collapsed dish frame the magnet visibly refuses, so the player learns the crane-cable limit early and reads it as a rule about the tool rather than a bug.

No piece is strictly dominant. Density and slot cost stay anticorrelated: the small classes (kick motor casing, pressurant sphere, thruster quad, ion grid) buy mass efficiency per slot at the price of raw value, while the mediums (truss, spar, gyro deck, fuel cell stack) pay better per grab and cost four slots uncrushed. Fragile pieces are the high-value-per-kilo end of both classes, so reaching for one is always a bet on the landing — and with uncrushable explicit per piece, that bet can never be bought off by a compactor tier.

What the slot table means, since it has now been asked twice: in the shipping slice every piece is one slot per GDD 4.3, and base_slots is a count of pieces. slots_crushed and slots_uncrushed describe the compactor and size-class content GDD 4.3 cut, and are emitted because the charter fixes them and the schema requires them. No mass figure in this file depends on a crush factor.

Altitudes are unchanged from the previous revision: spread on roughly 7 km centres across the full 50,000-280,000 m envelope and deliberately avoiding the Researcher's sample altitudes of 65,000, 115,000 and 215,000 m. The samples are where the sweep measures; a catalog that clustered there would be reintroducing three discrete bands under a continuous label.
